planting.note: Scatter seed onto bare shale scree or fine gravel in autumn so winter freeze-thaw cycles work it into crevices; plants overwinter as a basal rosette and bloom the following summer.

directions: This narrow endemic grows only on the loose, hot, acidic shale slopes of the central Appalachians, where it survives soil conditions too thin and unstable for most competitors. Lance-shaped grayish leaves give rise to pale yellow, four-petaled flowers that open in late afternoon and fade to a soft orange-pink by the next morning. Site it in a scree bed or crevice garden with sharp drainage and minimal organic matter, since rich or moisture-retentive soil invites rot and causes lush, floppy growth instead of the compact habit it shows in the wild. Once established on a lean, rocky slope it self-sows modestly and needs no supplemental feeding.

planting.note: Divide established clumps or set rooted cuttings in early spring into gritty, sharply drained soil on an open slope; seed requires a long cold stratification and is slow and uneven to germinate.

directions: Buckley's phlox is restricted to open shale barrens of Virginia and West Virginia, where loose, crumbling rock and intense summer heat keep out most other plants. It forms a low, woody-based mat of narrow needle-like leaves topped in late spring by clusters of pink to rose-purple flowers with notched petals, resembling a more delicate moss phlox. Plant it on a sunny, sharply drained slope or raised scree bed and resist the urge to mulch heavily, since good air circulation around the crown and lean, mineral soil mimic the shale habitat it needs to persist. It is a long-lived but slow-spreading choice for rock gardens and makes an excellent companion for other shale-barren specialists.
sources: West Virginia Division of Natural Resources

planting.note: Start seed indoors after a 60-90 day cold stratification and transplant small plugs into sharply drained, mineral soil in spring, spacing plants to let the silvery cushions fill in without crowding.

directions: Silverling occurs in two widely separated habitats, alpine summits of the White Mountains and the hot, dry shale barrens of the mid-Appalachians, a striking disjunction that reflects its tolerance for thin, mineral-poor soil under extreme exposure. It forms a dense, silvery cushion of tiny overlapping leaves and papery bracts that catch the light, with inconspicuous flowers nearly hidden among the foliage in summer. Grow it in full sun in a scree or crevice garden with coarse gravel mixed into the root zone, and keep it well away from richer garden soil or standing moisture, which quickly rot the tightly packed crown. It is a slow-growing but long-lived specimen for collectors of true rock-garden rarities.

planting.note: Sow seed directly in fall onto loose shale fragments or gritty soil so it experiences a natural winter chill; seedlings emerge the following spring and the plant typically flowers in its second year.

directions: Mountain pimpernel is a true shale-barren specialist found on exposed, rubbly slopes of the central Appalachians, where it sends up slender, branching stems from a deep taproot adapted to dry, shifting rock. Flat-topped clusters of small yellow flowers appear in mid to late spring, giving it a delicate resemblance to golden Alexanders but with finer, more divided foliage. Plant it in full sun on a lean, fast-draining slope and avoid disturbing the taproot once it is established, since this species resents transplanting after its first season. It pairs well with other barren endemics and tolerates the kind of baking summer heat and winter freeze-thaw that would damage most garden perennials.
sources: West Virginia Division of Natural Resources

planting.note: Divide spreading basal rosettes in early spring and set into lean, gritty soil on an open slope; clumps knit together into a groundcover within a season or two.

directions: Shale-barren ragwort forms low, spreading rosettes of felted, silvery-white leaves that resemble pussytoes foliage, an adaptation that reflects intense sun and reduces moisture loss on bare shale outcrops. In mid-spring it sends up short stalks topped with small clusters of bright yellow daisy-like flowers that stand out against the gray rock and silver foliage below. Grow it in full sun in very well-drained, mineral soil, where it slowly spreads to form a tight groundcover useful for stabilizing dry, rocky slopes. It needs no feeding and performs poorly if given rich soil or regular watering, both of which encourage soft growth prone to rot.

planting.note: Direct sow scarified seed in early spring into thin, rocky soil on an open barren-like slope; established plants form a low mat that persists for years without replanting.

directions: Named for Kate's Mountain near White Sulphur Springs, West Virginia, this clover is restricted to a handful of shale-barren outcrops in the central Appalachians, where its deep root tolerates summer drought on bare, crumbling rock. It forms a low, tufted mat of narrow trifoliate leaflets and produces small, dense, creamy-white to pale pink flowerheads in late spring, smaller and tidier than common pasture clovers. Grow it in full sun on lean, rocky, well-drained soil and avoid fertilizing, since excess nitrogen pushes soft growth that struggles in the heat it is adapted to withstand. It is a fitting, low-maintenance choice for a dry rock garden themed around true barren endemics.
sources: West Virginia Division of Natural Resources
